edges.effect_quant: Large prospective and retrospective cohorts report recurrent Clostridioides difficile cure rates around 80% after FMT, but a 2025 placebo-controlled capsule trial in 153 veterans did not reduce recurrence or death by day 56.
edges.population: adults with recurrent or refractory Clostridioides difficile infection
edges.mechanism: FMT can restore colonization resistance by repopulating anaerobic commensals that suppress C. difficile outgrowth, normalize bile-acid metabolism, and promote mucosal recovery after repeated antibiotic disruption. Differences in delivery route, donor material, and the severity profile of enrolled patients likely explain part of the gap between positive real-world cohorts and the negative placebo-controlled capsule trial.
edges.summary: FMT remains a plausible and often effective option for recurrent C. difficile, but the modern evidence is not as one-directional as the older enthusiasm suggested. Real-world multicenter cohorts still show high cure rates, yet a recent randomized capsule trial failed to beat placebo on recurrence or death, so the fairest reading is that benefit is likely context-dependent rather than uniformly guaranteed.
edges.caveats: Delivery route, patient frailty, ongoing antibiotic exposure, and protocol differences matter a lot here. This edge should not be read as proof that every FMT product or capsule strategy works equally well, especially because the best controlled trial in a veteran population was neutral.
